steps.title: Even Intersections
steps.prompt:
Let [n]={1,2,...,n}, and let F be a family of distinct subsets of [n] such that:

1. every A in F has even cardinality, and
2. |A∩B| is even for every two distinct A,B in F.

Determine the maximum possible value of |F| as a function of n. Give a construction attaining the maximum and prove the upper bound. Finally, prove that every family attaining the maximum is closed under symmetric difference: if A,B are in F, then A△B is also in F.
steps.reference:
The maximum is 2^{floor(n/2)}.

Represent each subset A⊆[n] by its characteristic vector v_A in the vector space F_2^n. Under this correspondence, symmetric difference becomes vector addition, and

v_A·v_B = |A∩B| mod 2,

where the dot product is the standard bilinear form over F_2.

The hypotheses imply v_A·v_B=0 for all A,B in F. This includes A=B because v_A·v_A=|A| mod 2=0 by the even-cardinality condition.

Let W be the linear span over F_2 of the vectors v_A for A in F. By bilinearity, every two vectors in W are orthogonal: if x and y are linear combinations of vectors from F, then x·y is a sum of terms v_A·v_B, all of which are zero. Thus W is totally self-orthogonal, meaning W⊆W^⊥.

The standard dot product on F_2^n is nondegenerate, so dim(W)+dim(W^⊥)=n. Since W⊆W^⊥, we obtain

2 dim(W)≤n,

and hence dim(W)≤floor(n/2). Because F is a set of vectors contained in W,

|F|≤|W|=2^{dim(W)}≤2^{floor(n/2)}.

To attain the bound, put m=floor(n/2) and partition 2m elements into disjoint pairs, for example

{1,2},{3,4},...,{2m-1,2m}.

Let F consist of all unions of these m pairs; if n is odd, the remaining element is never used. There are 2^m such unions. Every member has even size. The intersection of two members is also a union of some of the same pairs, so its size is even. Therefore the bound is attained.

Finally, suppose |F|=2^m, where m=floor(n/2), and let W=span(F). Since F⊆W, we have

2^m=|F|≤|W|=2^{dim(W)}.

Thus dim(W)≥m. The upper-bound argument gives dim(W)≤m, so dim(W)=m and |W|=2^m. Since F⊆W and the two finite sets have equal size, F=W. Therefore F is a vector subspace of F_2^n. In particular, v_A+v_B belongs to F whenever v_A and v_B do. Vector addition corresponds to symmetric difference, so A△B belongs to F. This also shows that every extremal family necessarily contains the empty set.
rubric: Correctly obtains the bound |F|≤2^{floor(n/2)}, with a valid argument such as characteristic vectors over F_2, total self-orthogonality, and a dimension bound.
Gives a valid construction of size 2^{floor(n/2)}, such as all unions of floor(n/2) fixed disjoint pairs, and verifies both parity conditions.
Proves the equality claim rigorously: an extremal family equals its linear span and therefore is closed under symmetric difference.
steps.answer:
Answer  
Maximum size: |F| = 2^{n−1}.

Construction  
Fix one coordinate, say the last one, and take all subsets of [n] that contain an even number of the first n−1 elements:

F₀ = { A⊆[n] : |A∩[n−1]| is even }.

Every member of F₀ has even cardinality (because the parity of |A| equals the parity of |A∩[n−1]| + |A∩{n}|, and both summands have the same parity).  
For any two distinct A,B∈F₀ the intersection A∩B also has even cardinality, because the characteristic vectors of A∩[n−1] and B∩[n−1] are orthogonal over 𝔽₂.  
Hence F₀ satisfies the two conditions and |F₀| = 2^{n−1}.

Upper bound  
Work in the vector space V = 𝔽₂^{n}. Identify each subset A⊆[n] with its characteristic vector v_A∈V.  
The two conditions translate into:

1. v_A·v_A = 0 (even cardinality),  
2. v_A·v_B = 0 for A≠B (even intersection).

Thus the set {v_A : A∈F} is a self-orthogonal subset of V.  
A self-orthogonal set is linearly independent: a linear dependence  
∑_{A∈F} λ_A v_A = 0 (λ_A∈𝔽₂)  
implies, after taking the dot product with any v_B,  
0 = v_B·(∑ λ_A v_A) = λ_B (v_B·v_B) = λ_B·0 = λ_B,  
so every λ_B vanishes.  
Therefore |F| ≤ dim V = n.  
But we need the stronger bound 2^{n−1}.

Restrict to the subspace  
W = {x∈V : x·x = 0}.  
W has dimension n−1 (it is the kernel of the linear form x↦x·x).  
The same argument shows that the vectors {v_A : A∈F} are linearly independent in W, hence |F| ≤ dim W = 2^{n−1}.

Closure under symmetric difference  
Let F be any family achieving |F| = 2^{n−1}.  
The vectors {v_A : A∈F} form a basis of the (n−1)–dimensional space W, so they span W.  
In particular, for any two vectors v_A, v_B we have v_A + v_B ∈ W.  
But v_A + v_B is the characteristic vector of the symmetric difference A△B, and membership in W means exactly that A△B has even cardinality.  
Since the intersection of any set in F with A△B is even (because every vector in W is orthogonal to every v_C), the set A△B satisfies the two conditions.  
Therefore A△B is already one of the 2^{n−1} sets in F, i.e. F is closed under symmetric difference.
steps.steering_note: The candidate repeatedly finds the correct conclusion and useful structure but leaves central proof gaps, so this final question tests whether they can turn one key linear-algebraic insight into a complete extremal argument.

verdict.assessment: Correct final classifications were reached in Questions 1–4, but most proofs had substantial gaps. Q1’s revised weighing scheme contains opposite code pairs and the impossibility of 13 was only asserted. Q2’s forcing argument is invalid and the 8-vertex verification misstates degrees. Q3 has the right root-propagation idea but does not rigorously eliminate complex root cycles. Q4 is largely sound Vieta jumping, with a minor false strict-inequality claim at the base case. Q5 is a major failure: the claimed maximum and construction are wrong, and the linear-algebra argument confuses dimension with cardinality. Overall, the candidate recognizes several advanced methods but is unreliable at verification and rigorous completion.

steps.title: A Diophantine Descent
steps.prompt:
Determine all ordered pairs of positive integers (x, y) satisfying

x² + y² + 2 = 4xy.

Your answer must give an explicit description of every solution and prove that no others exist.
steps.reference:
Define a₀ = a₁ = 1 and, for n ≥ 1, define aₙ₊₁ = 4aₙ − aₙ₋₁. Thus the sequence begins 1, 1, 3, 11, 41, .... The complete set of ordered solutions is

(aₙ, aₙ₊₁) and (aₙ₊₁, aₙ) for every n ≥ 0.

First, all listed pairs are solutions. The pair (a₀,a₁)=(1,1) satisfies the equation. Moreover, the transformation (u,v) ↦ (v,4v−u) preserves the equation, because

v² + (4v−u)² + 2 − 4v(4v−u) = u² + v² + 2 − 4uv.

Thus induction shows that every consecutive pair (aₙ,aₙ₊₁) is a solution, and symmetry gives the reversed pairs. The recurrence also yields positive terms: after a₁, the sequence is strictly increasing, since a₂=3>a₁ and, if aₙ>aₙ₋₁>0, then aₙ₊₁=4aₙ−aₙ₋₁>3aₙ>0.

It remains to prove completeness. Let (x,y) be any positive integer solution, and by symmetry suppose x≤y. Regard the equation as a quadratic in y:

y² − 4xy + (x²+2)=0.

If y is one root, the other root is y′=4x−y. By the product-of-roots formula,

yy′=x²+2,

so y′ is a positive integer.

If x=y, the equation gives 2x²+2=4x², hence x=1, producing (1,1). Now suppose x<y. If x=1, then y²−4y+3=0, so y=3; this is the pair (1,3), whose descent gives y′=1. If x=2, then y²−8y+6=0, whose discriminant 40 is not a square, so there is no integer solution. If x≥3, then y≥x+1, and therefore

y′=(x²+2)/y ≤ (x²+2)/(x+1) < x,

where the final inequality is equivalent to 2<x. Hence (y′,x) is another positive solution whose maximum coordinate is strictly smaller than y.

Repeatedly applying this descent must terminate, and it can terminate only at (1,1), with the last nontrivial step passing through (1,3). Reversing the descent applies (u,v) ↦ (v,4v−u), so every original solution is a consecutive pair in the stated recurrence, up to swapping coordinates. Therefore the displayed list is complete.
rubric: Correctly identifies the full solution family, for example via the recurrence a₀=a₁=1 and aₙ₊₁=4aₙ−aₙ₋₁, including both coordinate orders.
Proves that every listed pair satisfies the equation, using induction or the invariant-preserving transformation (u,v) ↦ (v,4v−u).
Proves exhaustiveness with a valid descent, including positivity and strict decrease of the alternate root and correct handling of the small cases x=1 and x=2.
steps.answer:
Let  

\[
a_0=1,\qquad a_1=1,\qquad a_{n+2}=4a_{n+1}-a_n\ \ (n\ge 0).
\]

The first few terms are  

\[
1,\;1,\;3,\;11,\;41,\;153,\;571,\dots
\]

---

### Theorem
The positive integer solutions of  

\[
x^2+y^2+2=4xy\tag{1}
\]

are exactly the ordered pairs  

\[
(a_n,a_{n+1})\quad\text{and}\quad(a_{n+1},a_n)\qquad(n\ge 0).
\]

In particular the first solutions are  

\[
(1,1),\;(1,3),\;(3,1),\;(3,11),\;(11,3),\;(11,41),\;(41,11),\dots
\]

---

### Proof

#### 1.  Every listed pair is a solution
For \(n=0\) we have \((a_0,a_1)=(1,1)\) and \(1^2+1^2+2=4\cdot1\cdot1\).

Assume \((a_n,a_{n+1})\) satisfies (1).  Treat (1) as a quadratic in \(x\) with \(y=a_{n+1}\):

\[
x^2-4a_{n+1}x+(a_{n+1}^2+2)=0.
\]

One root is \(x=a_n\).  By Vieta’s formulas the other root is  

\[
x'=4a_{n+1}-a_n=a_{n+2}.
\]

Hence \((a_{n+1},a_{n+2})\) also satisfies (1).  By symmetry \((a_{n+2},a_{n+1})\) does as well.  Induction shows that every consecutive pair of the sequence (in either order) is a solution.

---

#### 2.  No other solutions exist
Let \((x,y)\) be any positive integer solution of (1) with \(x\ge y\).

If \(x=y\), then \(2x^2+2=4x^2\), so \(x^2=1\) and \((x,y)=(1,1)=(a_0,a_0)\).

Assume \(x>y\).  Consider the quadratic in \(t\)

\[
t^2-4yt+(y^2+2)=0.\tag{2}
\]

Since \(x\) is a root of (2), the other root is  

\[
x'=4y-x=\frac{y^2+2}{x}.
\]

Thus \(x'\) is a positive integer and \((x',y)\) is again a solution of (1).

We claim \(x'<y\).  Indeed,
\[
x'<y\iff \frac{y^2+2}{x}<y\iff y^2+2<xy.
\]
Because \(x>y\) and \(x,y\) are integers, \(x\ge y+1\).

* If \(y=1\), equation (1) becomes \(x^2-4x+3=0\), so \(x=3\); then \(x'=1=y\).
* If \(y=2\), the discriminant of (2) is \(12\cdot 2^2-8=40\), not a square, so there is no integer \(x\).
* If \(y\ge 3\), then \(xy\ge y(y+1)=y^2+y>y^2+2\), whence \(x'<y\).

Hence, unless \((x,y)=(3,1)\), the new solution \((x',y)\) has a strictly smaller maximum coordinate:
\[
\max(x',y)<x=\max(x,y).
\]
For \((3,1)\) we obtain \((1,1)\) in one step.  Repeating this “Vieta jumping” descent must therefore terminate at \((1,1)\).

Consequently every solution can be reduced to \((1,1)\) by finitely many steps of replacing the larger number by the smaller root of (2).  Reversing this process starting from \((1,1)\) means repeatedly applying the map  

\[
(u,v)\longmapsto (v,\,4v-u),
\]

which generates exactly the sequence \((a_n)\):
\[
(1,1)\to(1,3)\to(3,11)\to(11,41)\to\cdots
\]

Therefore any positive integer solution of (1) must be a pair of consecutive terms of \((a_n)\) in some order.

---

### Explicit closed form (optional)
The recurrence has characteristic equation \(r^2-4r+1=0\), with roots \(2\pm\sqrt3\).  Solving gives

\[
a_n=\frac{3-\sqrt3}{6}(2+\sqrt3)^n+\frac{3+\sqrt3}{6}(2-\sqrt3)^n,
\]

and the solution set of (1) is exactly \(\{(a_n,a_{n+1}),(a_{n+1},a_n)\mid n\ge0\}\).
steps.steering_note: With no prior evidence, this starts at a strong level and tests whether the candidate can discover a constructive pattern and prove its completeness by infinite descent.

steps.title: A Nonlinear Functional Equation
steps.prompt:
Determine all twice continuously differentiable functions f: ℝ → ℝ satisfying f′(0)=1 and

f(x−y)f(x+y)=f(x)²−f(y)²

for every pair of real numbers x and y. Prove that your list is complete.
steps.reference:
The complete list is

1. f(x)=x;
2. f(x)=sinh(ax)/a for any a>0;
3. f(x)=sin(ax)/a for any a>0.

Equivalently, these are the normalized solutions of f″=cf for arbitrary real constants c.

First, put y=0 in the functional equation. This gives

f(x)²=f(x)²−f(0)²,

so f(0)=0.

Differentiate the equation twice with respect to y. At y=0, the second derivative of the left side is

2f(x)f″(x)−2f′(x)²,

while the second derivative of the right side is

−2(f′(0)²+f(0)f″(0))=−2.

Therefore

f(x)f″(x)−f′(x)²=−1.   (1)

Because f′(0)=1, there is ε>0 such that f′ is positive on (−ε,ε). Thus f is invertible there and f(x)≠0 for 0<|x|<ε.

On (0,ε), use t=f(x) as a local coordinate and define

q(t)=f′(f⁻¹(t))².

Then q′(t)=2f″(f⁻¹(t)). Equation (1) becomes

(t/2)q′(t)−q(t)=−1.

Solving this first-order linear equation gives

q(t)=1+ct²

for some real constant c. Returning to x and using (1),

f′(x)²=1+cf(x)²,

and hence

f(x)f″(x)=f′(x)²−1=cf(x)².

Since f(x)≠0 on (0,ε), it follows that

f″(x)=cf(x)

there.

The same constant applies on the negative side. Indeed, putting x=0 in the original equation gives

f(−y)f(y)=−f(y)².

For sufficiently small nonzero y, f(y)≠0, so f(−y)=−f(y). Thus f is locally odd, and the differential equation f″=cf extends to (−ε,ε).

With f(0)=0 and f′(0)=1, uniqueness for this constant-coefficient ODE gives, locally,

f(x)=x if c=0,

f(x)=sinh(ax)/a if c=a²>0,

and

f(x)=sin(ax)/a if c=−a²<0,

where a>0.

It remains to justify that this local identification is global. Differentiate the original functional equation once with respect to y:

−f′(x−y)f(x+y)+f(x−y)f′(x+y)=−2f(y)f′(y).

Set y=x. Since f(0)=0 and f′(0)=1, this yields the duplication identity

f(2x)=2f(x)f′(x).   (2)

Each of the three candidate functions, call it g, satisfies the same identity. If f=g on an interval (−R,R), then f′=g′ there, and for every |z|<2R, equation (2) with x=z/2 gives

f(z)=2f(z/2)f′(z/2)=2g(z/2)g′(z/2)=g(z).

Thus equality on (−R,R) implies equality on (−2R,2R). Starting from the local interval and iterating proves f=g on all of ℝ.

Finally, all listed functions satisfy f′(0)=1. Their functional equations follow respectively from

(x−y)(x+y)=x²−y²,

sinh(u−v)sinh(u+v)=sinh²u−sinh²v,

and

sin(u−v)sin(u+v)=sin²u−sin²v.

Therefore the list is complete.
rubric: Derives f(0)=0 and the differential identity f f″−(f′)²=−1 correctly.
Uses the identity rigorously to obtain a single local equation f″=cf and hence the three normalized local solution families.
Supplies a valid global-extension argument, such as deriving f(2x)=2f(x)f′(x), and verifies that every listed function satisfies the original equation.
steps.answer: None
steps.steering_note: The candidate gave a fully rigorous solution at 1750, including a correct descent and closed form, so the next question raises the difficulty and probes functional equations, calculus, and global completeness.

steps.title: A Matrix Commutator Characterization
steps.prompt:
Let A be an n×n real matrix. Prove that there exists an n×n real matrix B satisfying

AB − BA = A

if and only if A is nilpotent.
steps.reference:
Suppose first that AB−BA=A. We prove that A is nilpotent.

For every integer k≥1, the commutator product rule gives

[A^k,B]=A^{k-1}[A,B]+A^{k-2}[A,B]A+⋯+[A,B]A^{k-1},

where [X,Y]=XY−YX. Since [A,B]=A and A commutes with its powers, every term on the right is A^k. Hence

A^kB−BA^k=kA^k.

Taking traces and using tr(XY)=tr(YX), we obtain

0=tr(A^kB−BA^k)=k tr(A^k),

so tr(A^k)=0 for every k≥1, in particular for k=1,…,n.

Let λ_1,…,λ_n be the complex eigenvalues of A, counted with algebraic multiplicity. Then

λ_1^k+⋯+λ_n^k=tr(A^k)=0

for k=1,…,n. Newton's identities imply successively that every elementary symmetric polynomial e_1,…,e_n in the λ_i is zero: if p_k=Σ_i λ_i^k, then

k e_k=Σ_{i=1}^k (−1)^{i-1}e_{k-i}p_i,

with e_0=1, and every p_i here is zero. Thus the characteristic polynomial is t^n. By the Cayley–Hamilton theorem, A^n=0, so A is nilpotent.

Conversely, suppose A is nilpotent. Over the real numbers, a nilpotent matrix has a real Jordan form consisting of nilpotent Jordan blocks. It is therefore enough to construct B on each block and take the block-diagonal direct sum.

For a nilpotent Jordan block J_m with ones in positions (i,i+1), define

D_m=diag(0,1,2,…,m−1).

The only nonzero entries of J_mD_m−D_mJ_m occur in positions (i,i+1), and there they equal

(D_m)_{i+1,i+1}−(D_m)_{i,i}=i−(i−1)=1.

Therefore

J_mD_m−D_mJ_m=J_m.

If A=SJS^{-1}, where J is the block-diagonal Jordan form, let D be the block-diagonal matrix formed from the corresponding D_m and set B=SDS^{-1}. Then

AB−BA=S(JD−DJ)S^{-1}=SJS^{-1}=A.

Thus such a matrix B exists exactly when A is nilpotent.
rubric: Derives a valid identity such as [A^k,B]=kA^k and concludes that tr(A^k)=0 for sufficiently many powers.
Rigorously justifies that the vanishing power traces imply that A is nilpotent, for example using Newton identities and Cayley–Hamilton.
Proves the converse by constructing B on each nilpotent Jordan block, with the correct diagonal entries and commutator sign.
Handles arbitrary block sizes and conjugates the blockwise construction back to the original real basis.
steps.answer:
**Proof.**

*Only if.*  
Suppose there is a real matrix \(B\) with \(AB-BA=A\). We first show by induction that
\[
A^{k}B-BA^{k}=kA^{k}\qquad\text{for every integer }k\ge 1. \tag{1}
\]
For \(k=1\) this is the hypothesis.  Assuming (1) holds for \(k\),
\[
\begin{aligned}
A^{k+1}B
&=A\bigl(A^{k}B\bigr)
 =A\bigl(BA^{k}+kA^{k}\bigr)      &&\text{(induction hypothesis)}\\
&=(AB)A^{k}+kA^{k+1}
 =(BA+A)A^{k}+kA^{k+1}           &&\text{(since }AB=BA+A\text{)}\\
 &=BA^{k+1}+(k+1)A^{k+1}.
\end{aligned}
\]
Thus \(A^{k+1}B-BA^{k+1}=(k+1)A^{k+1}\), completing the induction.

Taking the trace of (1) gives \(k\,\operatorname{tr}(A^{k})=0\), so
\[
\operatorname{tr}(A^{k})=0\qquad\text{for all }k\ge 1.
\]
Let \(\lambda_{1},\dots ,\lambda_{n}\in\mathbb C\) be the eigenvalues of \(A\).  Then
\[
\lambda_{1}^{k}+\cdots +\lambda_{n}^{k}=0\qquad\text{for all }k\ge 1.
\]
If some \(\lambda_{i}\neq 0\), let \(\mu_{1},\dots ,\mu_{s}\) be the distinct non‑zero eigenvalues, with multiplicities \(m_{1},\dots ,m_{s}\).  Hence
\[
\sum_{j=1}^{s}m_{j}\mu_{j}^{k}=0\qquad(k=1,\dots ,s).
\]
This is a homogeneous linear system in the unknowns \(m_{j}\mu_{j}\) whose coefficient matrix is the Vandermonde matrix \((\mu_{j}^{\,k-1})_{j,k}\).  Because the \(\mu_{j}\) are distinct, that matrix is invertible, forcing \(m_{j}\mu_{j}=0\) for all \(j\), a contradiction.  Therefore every eigenvalue of \(A\) is \(0\); the characteristic polynomial of \(A\) is \(x^{n}\), and by Cayley–Hamilton \(A^{n}=0\).  Thus \(A\) is nilpotent.

*If.*  
Assume \(A\) is nilpotent.  Since \(0\) is a real eigenvalue, there exists an invertible real matrix \(P\) such that
\[
J=P^{-1}AP=\operatorname{diag}\bigl(J_{m_{1}}(0),\dots ,J_{m_{r}}(0)\bigr),
\]
where \(J_{m}(0)\) is the \(m\times m\) nilpotent Jordan block with \(1\)’s on the superdiagonal and \(0\)’s elsewhere.

For a single block \(J_{m}(0)\) set \(D_{m}=\operatorname{diag}(1,2,\dots ,m)\).  A direct entrywise check shows
\[
J_{m}(0)D_{m}-D_{m}J_{m}(0)=J_{m}(0),
\]
because the only non‑zero entries of the commutator are in positions \((i,i+1)\), where they equal \((i+1)-i=1\).

Now form the block‑diagonal matrix
\[
B_{J}=\operatorname{diag}\bigl(D_{m_{1}},\dots ,D_{m_{r}}\bigr).
\]
Then \(JB_{J}-B_{J}J=J\).  Define
\[
B=PB_{J}P^{-1}.
\]
It follows that
\[
AB-BA=P(JB_{J}-B_{J}J)P^{-1}=PJP^{-1}=A.
\]
Hence a real matrix \(B\) with the required property exists.

Therefore there exists a real \(n\times n\) matrix \(B\) satisfying \(AB-BA=A\) if and only if \(A\) is nilpotent. ∎
steps.steering_note: The candidate gave a polished, complete olympiad-level number-theory proof but did not answer the analytic question, so this probes comparably advanced reasoning in a finite algebraic setting.

steps.title: Variance of Peaks in a Random Permutation
steps.prompt: Let π be a uniformly random permutation of {1,2,...,n}, where n ≥ 4. An index i with 2 ≤ i ≤ n−1 is called a peak if π(i) is larger than both π(i−1) and π(i+1). Let X be the number of peaks. Find exact formulas for E[X] and Var(X), and justify all dependence or independence claims used in your derivation.
steps.reference:
For each interior index i, define I_i to be 1 if i is a peak and 0 otherwise. Then X = Σ_{i=2}^{n−1} I_i.

Among the three entries π(i−1), π(i), π(i+1), each is equally likely to be the largest, so P(I_i=1)=1/3. Therefore
E[X] = (n−2)/3.

For the variance, Var(I_i)=(1/3)(2/3)=2/9. We now compute covariances according to the distance between indices.

If j=i+1, the two indices cannot both be peaks, because I_i=1 requires π(i)>π(i+1), while I_{i+1}=1 requires π(i+1)>π(i). Thus
P(I_i=I_{i+1}=1)=0,
so Cov(I_i,I_{i+1})=0−1/9=−1/9.

If j=i+2, write the five relevant values as a,b,c,d,e, with peaks required at b and d. The conditions are b>a, b>c, d>c, and d>e. To compute their probability, represent the five relative ranks by independent continuous uniform variables. Conditional on c=x,
P(b>a and b>x | c=x) = ∫_x^1 b db = (1−x²)/2.
The analogous event d>e and d>x has the same probability, and the two events are conditionally independent given c. Hence
P(I_i=I_{i+2}=1) = ∫_0^1 ((1−x²)/2)^2 dx
= (1/4)(1−2/3+1/5)
= 2/15.
Therefore
Cov(I_i,I_{i+2}) = 2/15−1/9 = 1/45.

If |i−j|≥3, the triples of positions involved in I_i and I_j are disjoint. In a uniformly random permutation, the relative order patterns induced on disjoint sets of positions are independent: for any prescribed order on each set, all combinations occur equally often. Therefore I_i and I_j are independent, so their covariance is 0.

There are n−2 individual indicators, n−3 unordered adjacent pairs, and n−4 unordered pairs at distance 2. Thus
Var(X) = (n−2)(2/9) + 2(n−3)(−1/9) + 2(n−4)(1/45)
= 2(n+1)/45.

Therefore the exact formulas are
E[X] = (n−2)/3,
Var(X) = 2(n+1)/45.
rubric: Correctly introduces peak indicators and obtains E[X]=(n−2)/3.
Correctly computes covariance −1/9 for adjacent candidate peaks and 1/45 for peaks two positions apart.
Correctly justifies independence for indices at distance at least 3, rather than merely asserting that distant events are independent.
Counts each type of pair correctly and derives Var(X)=2(n+1)/45.
steps.answer:
Let
\[
I_i=\mathbf 1\{\text{$i$ is a peak}\},\qquad 2\le i\le n-1,
\]
so \(X=\sum_{i=2}^{n-1} I_i\).

## 1) \(\mathbb E[X]\)

For a fixed \(i\in\{2,\dots,n-1\}\), the triple
\[
\big(\pi(i-1),\pi(i),\pi(i+1)\big)
\]
consists of three distinct numbers in uniformly random order. All \(3!=6\) relative orderings are equally likely, and \(i\) is a peak iff \(\pi(i)\) is the largest of the three. That happens in exactly 2 of the 6 orderings (the other two can be in either order), hence
\[
\mathbb P(I_i=1)=\frac{1}{3}.
\]
By linearity of expectation,
\[
\mathbb E[X]=\sum_{i=2}^{n-1}\mathbb E[I_i]=(n-2)\cdot \frac13=\boxed{\frac{n-2}{3}}.
\]

## 2) Dependence/independence facts needed for \(\mathrm{Var}(X)\)

### (a) If \(|i-j|\ge 3\), then \(I_i\) and \(I_j\) are independent (so \(\mathrm{Cov}(I_i,I_j)=0\)).

Reason: \(I_i\) depends only on the relative order within the set of positions \(\{i-1,i,i+1\}\), and \(I_j\) depends only on the relative order within \(\{j-1,j,j+1\}\). When \(|i-j|\ge 3\) these position-sets are disjoint.

Formally, let \(A,B\) be disjoint position-sets. In a uniformly random permutation, conditional on the *sets of values* \(\{\pi(a):a\in A\}\) and \(\{\pi(b):b\in B\}\), the orders of those values within \(A\) and within \(B\) are independent and each uniformly random over all internal permutations. Since the “peak” event for a triple depends only on the internal relative order (not on the actual values), it follows that \(I_i\) and \(I_j\) are independent.

### (b) Adjacent indices cannot both be peaks: \(I_i I_{i+1}\equiv 0\).

If \(i\) is a peak then \(\pi(i)>\pi(i+1)\). If \(i+1\) were also a peak we would need \(\pi(i+1)>\pi(i)\), a contradiction. Hence
\[
\mathbb P(I_i=1,\,I_{i+1}=1)=0.
\]

### (c) For distance 2, \(\mathbb P(I_i=1,\,I_{i+2}=1)=\frac{2}{15}\).

This depends only on the relative order of the 5-tuple
\[
(a,b,c,d,e)=(\pi(i-1),\pi(i),\pi(i+1),\pi(i+2),\pi(i+3)),
\]
which is uniform over all \(5!=120\) orderings. The event \(\{I_i=1,I_{i+2}=1\}\) is the system of inequalities
\[
b>a,\quad b>c,\quad d>c,\quad d>e.
\]
Counting linear extensions of this partial order gives 16 satisfying orderings (a short recursion by “currently minimal elements” yields \(16\)), hence
\[
\mathbb P(I_i=1,\,I_{i+2}=1)=\frac{16}{120}=\frac{2}{15}.
\]

## 3) \(\mathrm{Var}(X)\)

We use
\[
\mathrm{Var}(X)=\sum_{i=2}^{n-1}\mathrm{Var}(I_i)+2\sum_{2\le i<j\le n-1}\mathrm{Cov}(I_i,I_j).
\]

- Single-site variance:
\[
\mathrm{Var}(I_i)=\frac13\Big(1-\frac13\Big)=\frac{2}{9}.
\]
There are \(n-2\) terms, so \(\sum \mathrm{Var}(I_i)=(n-2)\cdot \frac{2}{9}\).

- Covariances:
  * If \(|i-j|\ge 3\): covariance \(0\) by independence (2a).
  * If \(j=i+1\): using (2b),
    \[
    \mathrm{Cov}(I_i,I_{i+1})=0-\frac13\cdot\frac13=-\frac{1}{9}.
    \]
    There are \((n-3)\) such pairs.
  * If \(j=i+2\): using (2c),
    \[
    \mathrm{Cov}(I_i,I_{i+2})=\frac{2}{15}-\frac13\cdot\frac13=\frac{2}{15}-\frac19=\frac{1}{45}.
    \]
    There are \((n-4)\) such pairs.

Therefore
\[
\mathrm{Var}(X)=(n-2)\frac{2}{9}+2\Big((n-3)\Big(-\frac19\Big)+(n-4)\frac{1}{45}\Big).
\]
A quick simplification gives
\[
\mathrm{Var}(X)=\frac{2(n+1)}{45}.
\]

## Final formulas
\[
\boxed{\mathbb E[X]=\frac{n-2}{3}},\qquad
\boxed{\mathrm{Var}(X)=\frac{2(n+1)}{45}},\qquad (n\ge 4).
\]
steps.steering_note: With no prior evidence, this starts near the capable-to-frontier boundary and tests whether the candidate can combine indicator variables, local dependence, and exact probability calculations.

steps.title: Classifying Markov Triples
steps.prompt:
Classify all triples of positive integers (x,y,z) satisfying

x² + y² + z² = 3xyz.

More precisely, prove that every such triple can be obtained from (1,1,1) by repeatedly applying either of the following operations:

1. Permute the three coordinates.
2. Replace one coordinate by the other root of the corresponding quadratic; for example,
   (x,y,z) → (x,y,3xy − z).

Your proof must establish both directions: that these operations preserve positive-integer solutions, and that every positive-integer solution can be reduced to (1,1,1).
steps.reference:
Call a positive-integer solution a Markov triple.

First, the stated operations preserve positive-integer solutions. Permutations clearly do. Suppose (x,y,z) is a solution and put z′ = 3xy − z. Viewing the equation as a quadratic in z gives

z² − 3xyz + x² + y² = 0.

Its two roots are z and z′, so

z + z′ = 3xy,
zz′ = x² + y².

Thus z′ is an integer, and because z > 0 and zz′ = x² + y² > 0, it is also positive. Since z′ is the other root of the same quadratic, (x,y,z′) satisfies the original equation. The mutation is involutive, because 3xy − z′ = z.

It remains to prove that every solution can be reduced to (1,1,1). Given a solution, permute its coordinates so that

x ≤ y ≤ z.

Again consider

f(t) = t² − 3xyt + x² + y².

Its roots are z and z′ = 3xy − z. We know z′ is a positive integer. Evaluate f at y:

f(y) = x² + 2y² − 3xy² = x² − (3x − 2)y².

If x ≥ 2, then 3x − 2 ≥ 4 and y ≥ x, so

f(y) ≤ x² − 4y² < 0.

If x = 1, then

f(y) = 1 − y²,

which is negative unless y = 1.

Suppose first that f(y) < 0. Since f(0) = x² + y² > 0 and f is an upward-opening quadratic, y lies strictly between its two positive roots. Because z ≥ y and f(y) ≠ 0, z is the larger root. Therefore

0 < z′ < y ≤ z.

Replacing z by z′ consequently produces another positive-integer solution with strictly smaller coordinate sum.

The only remaining case is x = y = 1. Substitution gives

1 + 1 + z² = 3z,

or

z² − 3z + 2 = 0,

so z ∈ {1,2}. The triple (1,1,1) is the desired base triple, while (1,1,2) mutates in its largest coordinate to

(1,1,3·1·1 − 2) = (1,1,1).

Thus every non-base solution admits, after ordering its coordinates, a mutation that strictly decreases the positive integer x+y+z. Infinite descent is impossible, so repeated descent must terminate, and the preceding argument shows that it can terminate only at (1,1,1).

Reversing the descent steps shows that every positive-integer solution is obtained from (1,1,1) by coordinate permutations and mutations. Conversely, the first part showed that every triple so obtained remains a positive-integer solution. Hence the positive solutions are exactly the orbit of (1,1,1) under these operations.
rubric: Correctly proves that a mutation such as z → 3xy − z is integral, positive, equation-preserving, and involutive.
After ordering x ≤ y ≤ z, constructs a valid descent by proving that the mutated coordinate is smaller, including careful treatment of the exceptional case x = y = 1.
Uses well-founded descent to conclude that every solution reaches (1,1,1), and explicitly reverses the argument to obtain the requested classification in both directions.
steps.answer:
Let \((x,y,z)\in \mathbb Z_{>0}^3\) satisfy
\[
x^2+y^2+z^2=3xyz. \tag{1}
\]
Such triples are called **Markov triples**.

---

## 1) The two operations preserve positive-integer solutions

### (a) Permutations
Equation (1) is symmetric in \(x,y,z\), so permuting coordinates clearly preserves the set of solutions.

### (b) Vieta involution: \((x,y,z)\mapsto (x,y,3xy-z)\)
Rewrite (1) as a quadratic in \(z\):
\[
z^2-3xyz+(x^2+y^2)=0. \tag{2}
\]
So \(z\) is a root of the quadratic \(t^2-3xy\,t+(x^2+y^2)=0\). By Vieta’s formulas, the *other* root is
\[
z' = 3xy - z,
\]
and the product of the roots is
\[
zz' = x^2+y^2. \tag{3}
\]
Hence \(z'\in\mathbb Z\) whenever \(z\in\mathbb Z\), and substituting \(z'\) into (2) shows \((x,y,z')\) also satisfies (1).

It remains to check \(z'>0\). From (1),
\[
3xyz=x^2+y^2+z^2>z^2 \quad\Rightarrow\quad 3xy>z \quad\Rightarrow\quad z'=3xy-z>0.
\]
So the move \((x,y,z)\mapsto(x,y,3xy-z)\) sends positive-integer solutions to positive-integer solutions.

Finally, note that this move is an **involution**:
\[
3xy-(3xy-z)=z,
\]
so it is reversible.

---

## 2) Every positive-integer solution reduces to \((1,1,1)\)

We prove a descent: unless \((x,y,z)=(1,1,1)\), applying the Vieta involution to the largest coordinate strictly decreases the sum \(x+y+z\). Repeating must terminate, and the only terminal triple is \((1,1,1)\).

### Step 1: A key lemma (\(z\ge 2y\) unless \((1,1,1)\))
Let \((x,y,z)\) be a solution and reorder so that
\[
x\le y\le z.
\]
**Lemma.** If \((x,y,z)\ne (1,1,1)\), then \(z\ge 2y\).

**Proof.** Suppose instead that \(z<2y\). Then
\[
x^2+y^2+z^2 < x^2+y^2+4y^2 = x^2+5y^2 \le 6y^2
\]
(using \(x\le y\)). By (1),
\[
3xyz = x^2+y^2+z^2 < 6y^2 \quad\Rightarrow\quad xz < 2y.
\]
But \(z\ge y\), so \(xz\ge xy\), hence
\[
xy < 2y \quad\Rightarrow\quad x<2 \quad\Rightarrow\quad x=1.
\]
With \(x=1\), equation (1) becomes
\[
1+y^2+z^2 = 3yz.
\]
Treating this as a quadratic in \(z\),
\[
z^2 - 3y z + (y^2+1)=0,
\]
whose larger root is
\[
z=\frac{3y+\sqrt{5y^2-4}}{2}. \tag{4}
\]
If \(y\ge 2\), then \(\sqrt{5y^2-4} > y\), so (4) gives
\[
z>\frac{3y+y}{2}=2y,
\]
contradicting \(z<2y\). Therefore \(y=1\). Then \(1+1+z^2=3z\), i.e.
\[
z^2-3z+2=0 \implies z\in\{1,2\}.
\]
But \(z<2y=2\) forces \(z=1\). Thus \((x,y,z)=(1,1,1)\). ∎

So for any solution ordered \(x\le y\le z\), either it is \((1,1,1)\) or else \(z\ge 2y\).

---

### Step 2: Applying Vieta to the largest coordinate decreases the sum
Assume \(x\le y\le z\) and \((x,y,z)\ne (1,1,1)\). Let
\[
z' := 3xy - z.
\]
By (3),
\[
z'=\frac{x^2+y^2}{z}.
\]
Using \(x\le y\) and the lemma \(z\ge 2y\),
\[
z'=\frac{x^2+y^2}{z}\le \frac{2y^2}{2y}=y.
\]
Also, since \(z\ge 2y>y\), we get \(z'<z\). Therefore the new triple \((x,y,z')\) has strictly smaller sum:
\[
x+y+z' < x+y+z.
\]
It is still a positive-integer solution by Part 1.

Now reorder the new triple so it again satisfies \(x\le y\le z\), and repeat.

Because the sum is a positive integer and strictly decreases each time, this process must stop. It can only stop at a solution for which the “largest-coordinate Vieta move” does **not** decrease the sum; but we just proved that happens only for \((1,1,1)\). Hence:

**Every positive-integer solution can be reduced to \((1,1,1)\)** by repeatedly permuting to make the largest coordinate last and then applying \((x,y,z)\mapsto(x,y,3xy-z)\) to that coordinate.

---

## 3) Every solution is obtained from \((1,1,1)\) by the operations

Take any positive-integer solution \((x,y,z)\). By Part 2 there is a finite sequence of allowed moves sending it to \((1,1,1)\). Every move in the allowed list is reversible:

- permutations invert by inverse permutations;
- \((x,y,z)\mapsto(x,y,3xy-z)\) is an involution.

Therefore reversing the reduction sequence gives a finite sequence of allowed moves taking \((1,1,1)\) to \((x,y,z)\).

So:

- the operations preserve positive-integer solutions, and
- every positive-integer solution lies in the orbit of \((1,1,1)\) under these operations.

This completes the classification.
steps.steering_note: The candidate gave a fully correct and carefully justified solution at 1650, so the next question raises the difficulty to a proof-intensive Diophantine classification requiring discovery and rigorous use of infinite descent.

steps.title: A Square Divisor of an Exponential
steps.prompt:
Determine all positive integers n such that

n² divides 2^n + 1.

Give a complete proof that your list contains every solution.
steps.reference:
The only solutions are n=1 and n=3.

Both work: 1² divides 2¹+1, and 3²=9 divides 2³+1=9.

Now suppose n² divides 2^n+1. Since 2^n+1 is odd, n must be odd.

Assume n>1, and let p be the smallest prime divisor of n. Since p divides n², we have
2^n ≡ -1 (mod p).
Let r be the multiplicative order of 2 modulo p. Then r divides 2n, because 2^{2n} ≡ 1 (mod p), but r does not divide n, because 2^n is not congruent to 1 modulo p. Since n is odd, this implies
r=2d
for some d dividing n. Also r divides p-1, so d<p.

If d>1, then d has a prime divisor that also divides n. By minimality of p, that prime divisor is at least p, contradicting d<p. Hence d=1 and r=2. Thus 2 ≡ -1 (mod p), so p divides 3 and therefore p=3. In particular, 3 divides n.

Write a=v_3(n). Because n is odd, the special case of the lifting-the-exponent identity gives
v_3(2^n+1)=v_3(2+1)+v_3(n)=1+a.
For completeness, this identity here can be seen directly. Write n=3^a u with 3 not dividing u. Since u is odd and not divisible by 3, u is congruent to 1 or 5 modulo 6, and consequently 2^u+1 is divisible by 3 but not by 9. Each replacement of an odd exponent t by 3t adds exactly one factor of 3, because
x^3+1=(x+1)(x^2-x+1)
and, when x ≡ -1 (mod 3), one has x^2-x+1 ≡ 3 (mod 9). Hence v_3(2^n+1)=1+a.

But n² divides 2^n+1, so
2a ≤ v_3(2^n+1)=1+a,
which gives a≤1. Since 3 divides n, a=1. Therefore n=3m where 3 does not divide m.

Suppose for contradiction that m>1, and let q be the smallest prime divisor of m. Thus q>3, and q is the smallest prime divisor of n other than 3. Again, because q divides 2^n+1, the order of 2 modulo q has the form
ord_q(2)=2d,
where d divides n; moreover 2d divides q-1, so d<q.

Every prime divisor of d is therefore a prime divisor of n smaller than q. By the choice of q, the only possibility is 3. Since v_3(n)=1 and d divides n, it follows that d is either 1 or 3.

If d=1, then ord_q(2)=2, so 2 ≡ -1 (mod q), forcing q to divide 3, impossible because q>3.

If d=3, then ord_q(2)=6. In particular 2^3 ≡ -1 (mod q), so q divides 2^3+1=9, again forcing q=3, a contradiction.

Thus m=1, so n=3. Together with n=1, the complete solution set is
{1,3}.
rubric: Correctly shows that any nontrivial solution is odd and uses the least prime divisor together with multiplicative order to prove that 3 is the least prime divisor.
Correctly proves or validly invokes v_3(2^n+1)=1+v_3(n) for odd n, and deduces that 3 divides n exactly once.
Excludes every additional prime divisor by applying the order argument to the least prime q>3, and explicitly verifies n=1 and n=3.
steps.answer: None
steps.steering_note: The candidate gave two flawless, rigorous solutions through difficulty 1880, so the next question moves to a less scaffolded high-olympiad number-theory classification requiring multiplicative orders, valuations, and a carefully chosen minimal prime.

steps.title: Optimal Counterfeit-Coin Strategy
steps.prompt:
You have N visually identical coins. Exactly one is counterfeit and is either heavier or lighter than every genuine coin; you do not know which coin it is or whether it is heavier or lighter. A balance scale has three possible outcomes: left pan heavier, balance, or right pan heavier. In every weighing, the same number of coins must be placed on each pan, and later weighings may depend on earlier outcomes.

What is the largest N for which the counterfeit coin and whether it is heavier or lighter can always be determined in three weighings? Prove optimality and give a complete strategy attaining the maximum.
steps.reference:
The maximum is N = 12.

OPTIMALITY

Suppose the first weighing places k coins on each pan. If the left pan is heavier, the counterfeit must be either one of the k coins on the left and heavy, or one of the k coins on the right and light. Thus this outcome leaves 2k possible states. The right-heavy outcome likewise leaves 2k states.

If the first weighing balances, the counterfeit is among the N−2k unweighed coins, each of which may be either heavy or light, leaving 2(N−2k) states.

Only two weighings remain after any first outcome, and two balance-scale weighings have at most 3^2 = 9 possible outcome sequences. Consequently every branch must contain at most nine states. Hence

2k ≤ 9,
2(N−2k) ≤ 9.

The first inequality gives k ≤ 4. The second gives N ≤ 2k + 4.5. Since N is an integer and k ≤ 4, this implies N ≤ 12.

STRATEGY FOR 12 COINS

Label the coins 1 through 12. First weigh

1,2,3,4 against 5,6,7,8.

Case 1: The first weighing balances.

Then coins 1 through 8 are genuine, and the counterfeit is among 9,10,11,12. Weigh

9,10,11 against 1,2,3.

If this balances, coin 12 is counterfeit; weigh 12 against coin 1 to determine whether it is heavy or light.

If the left pan is heavier, one of 9,10,11 is heavy. Weigh 9 against 10. If one side is heavier, that coin is the heavy counterfeit; if they balance, coin 11 is the heavy counterfeit.

If the left pan is lighter, one of 9,10,11 is light. Weigh 9 against 10. If one side is lighter, that coin is the light counterfeit; if they balance, coin 11 is the light counterfeit.

Case 2: The first weighing is unbalanced.

Let a1,a2,a3,a4 denote the four coins on the heavier pan, so these are candidates to be heavy. Let b1,b2,b3,b4 denote the four coins on the lighter pan, so these are candidates to be light. Coins 9 through 12 are genuine. This notation covers either direction of the first imbalance.

For the second weighing, weigh

a1,a2,b1 against a3,b2,9.

If the left pan is heavier, the possible states are a1 heavy, a2 heavy, or b2 light. Weigh a1 against a2. If one is heavier, it is the counterfeit; if they balance, b2 is the light counterfeit.

If the right pan is heavier, the possible states are a3 heavy or b1 light. Weigh a3 against genuine coin 9. If a3 is heavier, it is the heavy counterfeit; if they balance, b1 is the light counterfeit.

If the second weighing balances, the possible states are a4 heavy, b3 light, or b4 light. Weigh b3 against b4. If they balance, a4 is the heavy counterfeit; otherwise the lighter of b3 and b4 is the counterfeit.

Thus 12 coins can always be resolved in three weighings, while the counting argument proves that 13 cannot. Therefore the largest possible N is 12.
rubric: Proves the upper bound N ≤ 12 by analyzing all three branches of an equal-count first weighing and applying the nine-leaf bound for the two remaining weighings.
Gives a valid three-weighing strategy for all 12 coins, including the balanced first-weighing branch.
Completely handles both directions of an unbalanced first weighing and identifies both the counterfeit coin and whether it is heavy or light.
steps.answer:
## Maximum \(N\): \(12\)

### Optimality (why \(N\le 12\))
In the first weighing you must put the same number \(a\) of coins on each pan.

- If the scale **balances**, then every one of the \(2a\) weighed coins is genuine, so the counterfeit is among the \(N-2a\) unweighed coins, and it could be **heavy or light**:
\[
\#\text{possibilities in balance-branch}=2(N-2a).
\]

- If the scale is **unbalanced**, then the counterfeit is among the \(2a\) coins on the pans. Moreover, the direction of tipping tells you its “polarity”: it must be either
  - on the heavier side and heavy, or
  - on the lighter side and light.
So there are exactly \(a+a=2a\) possibilities in that branch:
\[
\#\text{possibilities in an unbalance-branch}=2a.
\]

After the first weighing, you have **two** weighings left, hence at most \(3^2=9\) outcome-patterns to distinguish possibilities in any branch. Therefore both branch sizes must be \(\le 9\):
\[
2a\le 9 \quad\Rightarrow\quad a\le 4,
\]
\[
2(N-2a)\le 9 \quad\Rightarrow\quad N-2a\le 4.
\]
With \(a\le 4\), the best you can do is \(a=4\), giving
\[
N \le 2a+4 = 12.
\]
So **no strategy can always succeed for \(N\ge 13\)**. Hence the maximum possible is **\(N=12\)**.

It remains to give a strategy that succeeds for \(12\).

---

## Strategy achieving \(N=12\) in three weighings

Label the coins \(1,2,\dots,12\).

### Weighing 1
Weigh:
\[
1234 \;\text{ vs }\; 5678.
\]

There are three cases.

---

## Case A: Weighing 1 balances
Then coins \(1\)–\(8\) are genuine, and the counterfeit is among \(9,10,11,12\), heavy or light.

### Weighing 2
Weigh:
\[
91011 \;\text{ vs }\; 123
\]
(where \(1,2,3\) are genuine).

- **If it balances**, then \(9,10,11\) are genuine, so coin \(12\) is counterfeit.

  ### Weighing 3
  Weigh:
  \[
  12 \text{ vs } 1.
  \]
  If \(12\) is heavier, it’s heavy; if lighter, it’s light.

- **If left is heavier**, then one of \(9,10,11\) is **heavy**.

  ### Weighing 3
  Weigh \(9\) vs \(10\).
  - If one side is heavier, that coin is the heavy counterfeit.
  - If they balance, then \(11\) is heavy.

- **If right is heavier**, then one of \(9,10,11\) is **light**.

  ### Weighing 3
  Weigh \(9\) vs \(10\).
  - If one side is lighter, that coin is the light counterfeit.
  - If they balance, then \(11\) is light.

This completes Case A.

---

## Case B: Weighing 1: left heavier \((1234>5678)\)
Then the counterfeit is either
- one of \(1,2,3,4\) and **heavy**, or
- one of \(5,6,7,8\) and **light**.
Coins \(9,10,11,12\) are genuine references.

### Weighing 2
Weigh:
\[
125 \;\text{ vs }\; 369
\]
(\(9\) is genuine).

Now analyze outcomes:

- **If left is heavier**, possibilities are exactly:
  \[
  1\text{ heavy},\;2\text{ heavy},\;6\text{ light}.
  \]
  ### Weighing 3
  Weigh \(1\) vs \(2\).
  - If left heavier: \(1\) is heavy.
  - If right heavier: \(2\) is heavy.
  - If balance: \(6\) is light.

- **If right is heavier**, possibilities are exactly:
  \[
  3\text{ heavy},\;5\text{ light}.
  \]
  ### Weighing 3
  Weigh \(5\) vs \(9\) (genuine).
  - If \(5\) is lighter: \(5\) is light.
  - If they balance: \(3\) is heavy.

- **If it balances**, possibilities are exactly:
  \[
  4\text{ heavy},\;7\text{ light},\;8\text{ light}.
  \]
  ### Weighing 3
  Weigh \(7\) vs \(8\).
  - If left heavier: \(8\) is light.
  - If right heavier: \(7\) is light.
  - If balance: \(4\) is heavy.

This completes Case B.

---

## Case C: Weighing 1: right heavier \((1234<5678)\)
This is symmetric: now the counterfeit is either
- one of \(5,6,7,8\) and **heavy**, or
- one of \(1,2,3,4\) and **light**,
with \(9,10,11,12\) genuine.

### Weighing 2
Weigh:
\[
561 \;\text{ vs }\; 729
\]
(\(9\) genuine).

- **If left is heavier**, possibilities:
  \[
  5\text{ heavy},\;6\text{ heavy},\;2\text{ light}.
  \]
  ### Weighing 3
  Weigh \(5\) vs \(6\).
  - If left heavier: \(5\) heavy.
  - If right heavier: \(6\) heavy.
  - If balance: \(2\) light.

- **If right is heavier**, possibilities:
  \[
  7\text{ heavy},\;1\text{ light}.
  \]
  ### Weighing 3
  Weigh \(1\) vs \(9\).
  - If \(1\) is lighter: \(1\) light.
  - If they balance: \(7\) heavy.

- **If it balances**, possibilities:
  \[
  8\text{ heavy},\;3\text{ light},\;4\text{ light}.
  \]
  ### Weighing 3
  Weigh \(3\) vs \(4\).
  - If left heavier: \(4\) light.
  - If right heavier: \(3\) light.
  - If balance: \(8\) heavy.

This completes Case C.

---

## Conclusion
- The optimality argument forces \(N\le 12\).
- The decision tree above correctly identifies, for \(N=12\), **which coin** is counterfeit and **whether it is heavy or light** in at most **three** weighings.

Therefore the largest such \(N\) is \(\boxed{12}\).
steps.steering_note: The candidate gave two strong, polished proofs but then no substantive answer to a harder number-theory problem, so this probes robust constructive reasoning and optimality at a slightly lower difficulty.

steps.title: An Integral Quotient and Vieta Descent
steps.prompt:
Determine all positive integers k for which there exist positive integers a,b satisfying

(a^2+b^2)/(ab+1) = k.

Prove both that every attainable k has the required form and that every k of that form is actually attained.
steps.reference:
The attainable values are exactly the positive perfect squares.

First prove necessity. Suppose, for contradiction, that a nonsquare positive integer k is attained. Among all positive-integer pairs (a,b) satisfying

a^2+b^2=k(ab+1),

choose one minimizing a+b, and by symmetry assume a>=b. Since k is a positive nonsquare integer, k>=2.

Regard the equation as a quadratic in a:

f(t)=t^2-kbt+(b^2-k).

One integer root is a, so the other root is

a'=kb-a,

which is also an integer. Vieta's formulas give

aa'=b^2-k.  (1)

We first show b^2>k. If instead b^2<=k, then (1) implies a'<=0. Put c=-a'=a-kb>=0. Equation (1) becomes

ac=k-b^2.

If c>=1, then a=kb+c>=kb+1, so

ac>=a>=kb+1>=k+1,

whereas k-b^2<=k-1 because b>=1. This is impossible. Therefore c=0, and then ac=k-b^2 gives k=b^2, contradicting the assumption that k is not a square. Hence b^2>k.

It follows from (1) that a'>0. We next show a'<b. We have

f(0)=b^2-k>0,

while

f(b)=b^2-kb^2+b^2-k=(2-k)b^2-k<0

for every k>=2. Thus b lies strictly between the two real roots of f. Since a>=b and a is a root, a is the larger root, while the other root satisfies

0<a'<b.

Because a' is the other root of the same quadratic, (a',b) is another positive-integer solution:

(a')^2+b^2=k(a'b+1).

But a'<b<=a, so a'+b<a+b, contradicting the minimal choice of (a,b). Therefore no nonsquare k can be attained, and every attainable k is a positive perfect square.

For sufficiency, let k=m^2 for any positive integer m. Choose

a=m,  b=m^3.

Then

(a^2+b^2)/(ab+1)=(m^2+m^6)/(m^4+1)=m^2(m^4+1)/(m^4+1)=m^2=k.

Thus every positive perfect square is attained. Hence the complete set of possible values is

{k: k=m^2 for some positive integer m}.
rubric: Correctly concludes that the attainable values are exactly the positive perfect squares and supplies a valid construction for every square.
For necessity, sets up a minimal-counterexample or equivalent Vieta-jumping argument and correctly introduces the other root a'=kb-a with aa'=b^2-k.
Rigourously handles the crucial case b^2<=k, showing it would force k=b^2, and then proves that when b^2>k the other root is a positive integer strictly smaller than b.
Clearly explains why the new pair remains a positive-integer solution and contradicts minimality, with no unjustified positivity or ordering assumptions.

steps.title: Permutations Without Consecutive Neighbors
steps.prompt: A permutation of the numbers 1,2,3,4,5,6,7 is chosen uniformly at random. What is the exact probability that no two numerically consecutive numbers appear next to each other in the permutation? For example, 4 and 5 may not occupy adjacent positions in either order. Give a rigorous derivation, not just the final probability.
steps.reference:
For i=1,...,6, let A_i be the event that i and i+1 are adjacent. We count permutations avoiding all six events by inclusion–exclusion.

Take a subset S of k of the six edges 1-2,2-3,...,6-7. Suppose those selected edges form c connected runs along this path. Each run forces all its involved numbers to form one contiguous block. A run has exactly two possible internal orders: increasing or decreasing. Contracting all k selected edges leaves 7-k objects, so the number of permutations satisfying every adjacency in S is

2^c(7-k)!.

It remains to count edge subsets with k selected edges arranged in c nonempty runs among six linearly ordered edge positions. This number is

C(k-1,c-1) C(7-k,c).

Indeed, C(k-1,c-1) chooses the positive lengths of the c runs, and C(7-k,c) distributes the 6-k unselected edges into the c-1 mandatory internal gaps and the two optional end gaps.

Thus the desired count is

7! + sum_{k=1}^6 (-1)^k (7-k)! sum_c C(k-1,c-1)C(7-k,c)2^c.

Evaluating by k:

k=0: 5040.
k=1: 6·2·6! = 8640.
k=2: 5·2·5! + 10·4·5! = 1200+4800=6000.
k=3: 4·2·4! + 12·4·4! + 4·8·4! = 192+1152+768? This last displayed arithmetic must be checked against the run count: for k=3,c=3 there are C(2,2)C(4,3)=4 subsets, each contributing 8·24=192, hence the contribution is 768. Therefore the full k=3 contribution is 192+1152+768=2112.

Continuing carefully:
k=4: c=1 gives 3·2·3!=36; c=2 gives 9·4·3!=216; c=3 gives 3·8·3!=144; total 396.
k=5: c=1 gives 2·2·2!=8; c=2 gives 4·4·2!=32; total 40.
k=6: c=1 gives 1·2·1!=2.

Hence the avoiding count is

5040-8640+6000-2112+396-40+2=646.

Therefore the exact probability is

646/5040 = 323/2520.

As a direct check of the delicate k=3 term: among 3-edge subsets of a 6-edge path, there are 4 with one run, 12 with two runs, and 4 with three runs, totaling C(6,3)=20, as required.
rubric: Defines the six forbidden adjacency events and applies inclusion–exclusion with the correct treatment of overlapping events.
Correctly explains that a selected edge set with k edges and c connected runs contributes 2^c(7-k)! permutations, and correctly counts such edge sets.
Obtains the exact favorable count 646 and probability 323/2520, with a rigorous derivation.

steps.title: Competing Coin Patterns
steps.prompt: A fair coin is flipped repeatedly until either HHT or THH appears as three consecutive outcomes. The process stops as soon as one of these patterns first appears. Determine exactly (i) the probability that HHT appears before THH, and (ii) the expected total number of flips until the process stops. Give a rigorous derivation.
steps.reference:
Track the longest suffix of the outcomes so far that is also a prefix of either target pattern. The relevant nonterminal states are S (empty suffix), H, HH, T, and TH.

First compute the probability of HHT winning. Let p_X be this probability starting from state X. The transitions give
p_S=(p_H+p_T)/2,
p_H=(p_HH+p_T)/2,
p_HH=(p_HH+1)/2,
p_T=(p_TH+p_T)/2,
p_TH=(0+p_T)/2.
Here, from HH a T completes HHT, while from TH an H completes THH. Solving, p_HH=1. The fourth equation gives p_T=p_TH, while the fifth gives p_TH=p_T/2, so p_T=p_TH=0. Therefore p_H=1/2 and
p_S=(1/2+0)/2=1/4.
Thus HHT appears first with probability 1/4.

Now let e_X be the expected number of additional flips until stopping from state X. First-step analysis gives
e_S=1+(e_H+e_T)/2,
e_H=1+(e_HH+e_T)/2,
e_HH=1+e_HH/2,
e_T=1+(e_TH+e_T)/2,
e_TH=1+e_T/2.
The absorbing outcomes contribute zero future flips. Solving, e_HH=2. Also e_T=2+e_TH and e_TH=1+e_T/2, hence e_T=6 and e_TH=4. Then e_H=1+(2+6)/2=5, so
e_S=1+(5+6)/2=13/2.
Therefore the exact answers are (i) 1/4 and (ii) 13/2 flips.
rubric: Obtains the exact probability 1/4 using valid state-based, recursive, or equivalently rigorous reasoning.
Obtains the expected stopping time 13/2 flips with the final stopping flip included.
Correctly handles pattern overlaps and explains the transitions or recurrences sufficiently to constitute a derivation.
steps.answer:
Let the sequence of flips be observed and stop as soon as either  
\(A=\text{HHT}\) or \(B=\text{THH}\) occurs.  
Because only the relevant suffix of the past flips can affect the future, we model the process by the longest suffix of the observed sequence that is a proper prefix of \(A\) or \(B\).

The proper prefixes of the two patterns are  
\(\varepsilon,\; H,\; T,\; HH,\; TH\).  
These form the transient states of a Markov chain.  
From each state we flip a fair coin once and move to the new longest such suffix; reaching \(A\) or \(B\) means absorption.

The transitions are:

| From | Flip H | Flip T |
|------|--------|--------|
| \(\varepsilon\) | \(H\) | \(T\) |
| \(H\) | \(HH\) | \(T\) |
| \(T\) | \(TH\) | \(T\) |
| \(HH\) | \(HH\) | **HHT** (absorbing) |
| \(TH\) | **THH** (absorbing) | \(T\) |

(For example, from \(H\) flipping \(T\) gives suffixes of \(HT\); the longest one that is a prefix of either pattern is \(T\).)

---

### (i) Probability that HHT appears before THH

Let \(p_s\) denote the probability that \(A=\text{HHT}\) occurs before \(B=\text{THH}\) when the current state is \(s\).  
Conditioning on the next flip gives the linear system

\[
\begin{aligned}
p_\varepsilon &= \tfrac12 p_H + \tfrac12 p_T,\\[2pt]
p_H &= \tfrac12 p_{HH} + \tfrac12 p_T,\\[2pt]
p_T &= \tfrac12 p_{TH} + \tfrac12 p_T,\\[2pt]
p_{HH} &= \tfrac12 p_{HH} + \tfrac12\cdot 1,\\[2pt]
p_{TH} &= \tfrac12\cdot 0 + \tfrac12 p_T .
\end{aligned}
\]

(The “\(1\)” in the \(HH\) equation corresponds to absorption in \(A\); the “\(0\)” in the \(TH\) equation corresponds to absorption in \(B\).)

From the fourth equation, \(\tfrac12 p_{HH}=\tfrac12\), so \(p_{HH}=1\).  
From the third equation, \(\tfrac12 p_T = \tfrac12 p_{TH}\), hence \(p_T=p_{TH}\).  
The fifth equation then gives \(p_{TH}=\tfrac12 p_T\), so \(p_T=\tfrac12 p_T\), yielding \(p_T=0\) and \(p_{TH}=0\).

Substituting into the second equation:
\[
p_H = \tfrac12(1) + \tfrac12(0) = \tfrac12 .
\]

Finally,
\[
p_\varepsilon = \tfrac12\!\left(\tfrac12\right) + \tfrac12(0) = \boxed{\tfrac14}.
\]

Thus \(\Pr(\text{HHT before THH}) = \tfrac14\) (and consequently \(\Pr(\text{THH before HHT}) = \tfrac34\)).

---

### (ii) Expected total number of flips until stopping

Let \(E_s\) be the expected remaining number of flips until absorption starting from state \(s\).  
Conditioning on the next flip (and counting that flip) gives

\[
\begin{aligned}
E_\varepsilon &= 1 + \tfrac12 E_H + \tfrac12 E_T,\\[2pt]
E_H &= 1 + \tfrac12 E_{HH} + \tfrac12 E_T,\\[2pt]
E_T &= 1 + \tfrac12 E_{TH} + \tfrac12 E_T,\\[2pt]
E_{HH} &= 1 + \tfrac12 E_{HH} + \tfrac12\cdot 0,\\[2pt]
E_{TH} &= 1 + \tfrac12\cdot 0

steps.title: A Diophantine Descent
steps.prompt:
Determine all ordered pairs of positive integers (x,y) satisfying

x^2 + y^2 + 1 = 3xy.

Your answer must give an explicit description of every solution and prove both that all listed pairs work and that no others exist.
steps.reference:
Define the integer sequence a_0=a_1=1 and

a_{n+1}=3a_n-a_{n-1}  for n>=1.

Thus the sequence begins 1,1,2,5,13,34,... . The complete set of ordered positive-integer solutions is

(x,y)=(a_n,a_{n+1}) or (a_{n+1},a_n),  for n>=0.

First prove that every listed pair works. The pair (a_0,a_1)=(1,1) satisfies the equation. More generally, if (u,v) satisfies

u^2+v^2+1=3uv,

then so does (v,3v-u), because

v^2+(3v-u)^2+1-3v(3v-u)
= u^2+v^2+1-3uv
=0.

The recurrence gives a_{n+1}=3a_n-a_{n-1}, so induction shows that every consecutive pair (a_n,a_{n+1}) satisfies the equation. The terms are positive: after a_1=1 and a_2=2, the recurrence gives a_{n+1}>a_n whenever a_n>a_{n-1}>0. Symmetry gives the reversed ordered pairs as well.

It remains to show that there are no other solutions. Let (x,y) be a positive-integer solution, and by symmetry suppose x<=y. If x=y, then

2x^2+1=3x^2,

so x=1 and the solution is (1,1).

Now suppose x<y. Regard the equation as a quadratic in y:

y^2-3xy+(x^2+1)=0.

Since one integer root is y, the other root is

z=3x-y=(x^2+1)/y.

Hence z is a positive integer, and Vieta's relations show that (z,x) also satisfies the original equation.

We show this is a descent. If x=1, the equation becomes y^2-3y+2=0, so y=2 because y>x; this is the solution (1,2), and z=1. If x>1, let

f(t)=t^2-3xt+x^2+1.

Its roots are z and y. Since

f(x)=1-x^2<0,

x lies strictly between the two roots. Because y>x, y is the larger root, and therefore 0<z<x<y. Thus replacing the sorted solution (x,y) by (z,x) strictly decreases its largest entry.

Repeating this descent must eventually reach (1,1); the final nontrivial step is (1,2) to (1,1). Reversing the descent is forced: from a consecutive pair (u,v), the next larger entry is 3v-u. Starting with 1,1 therefore produces exactly

(1,1), (1,2), (2,5), (5,13), ...,

which are the consecutive pairs (a_n,a_{n+1}). Consequently the stated list contains every positive-integer solution.
rubric: States the complete classification, for example via a_0=a_1=1 and a_{n+1}=3a_n-a_{n-1}, including both coordinate orders.
Proves that every listed pair satisfies the equation, using the invariant transformation (u,v) -> (v,3v-u) or an equivalent argument.
Uses Vieta jumping or an equivalent rigorous descent to turn any non-base solution into a strictly smaller positive solution.
Handles the base cases and explains why reversing the descent yields exactly the stated sequence, thereby excluding all other solutions.

steps.title: A Square Divisibility Exponential Equation
steps.prompt: Determine all positive integers n such that n² divides 2^n + 1. Prove both that every integer you list works and that no others do.
steps.reference:
The only solutions are n = 1 and n = 3. They work because 1² divides 2¹ + 1 = 3, and 3² = 9 divides 2³ + 1 = 9.

Now suppose n > 1 is a solution. First, n must be odd, since 2^n + 1 is odd and therefore cannot be divisible by n² if n is even.

Let p be the smallest prime divisor of n. Since p divides n² and n² divides 2^n + 1, we have 2^n ≡ -1 (mod p). Let d be the multiplicative order of 2 modulo p. Then d divides 2n but does not divide n. Because n is odd, this means d = 2e for some e dividing n. Also d divides p - 1, so e < p. Every prime divisor of e is also a prime divisor of n and hence is at least p, by the minimality of p. Since e < p, this forces e = 1. Thus d = 2, so 2 ≡ -1 (mod p), giving p = 3. Therefore 3 divides n.

Write n = 3^a m, where a ≥ 1 and gcd(m,3) = 1. For odd n, the lifting-the-exponent formula gives v_3(2^n + 1) = v_3(2 + 1) + v_3(n) = 1 + a. Since n² divides 2^n + 1, we need v_3(2^n + 1) ≥ v_3(n²) = 2a. Hence a + 1 ≥ 2a, so a ≤ 1. Thus a = 1.

It remains to prove m = 1. Suppose instead that m > 1, and let q be the smallest prime divisor of m. Then q ≥ 5. As before, because q divides 2^n + 1, the order of 2 modulo q has the form 2e, where e divides n and 2e divides q - 1; in particular, e < q. Any prime divisor of e divides n. Apart from 3, every prime divisor of n comes from m and is at least q. Since e < q and n contains exactly one factor of 3, it follows that e is either 1 or 3.

If e = 1, then the order is 2, so q divides 2 + 1 = 3, impossible because q ≥ 5. If e = 3, then the order is 6, so 2³ ≡ -1 (mod q), implying q divides 2³ + 1 = 9, again impossible for q ≥ 5. Thus m cannot exceed 1.

Consequently n = 3. Together with the separately checked solution n = 1, all solutions are n ∈ {1,3}.
rubric: Correctly identifies and verifies exactly n = 1 and n = 3.
Uses the least prime divisor and multiplicative order rigorously to prove that every nontrivial solution is divisible by 3.
Uses the 3-adic valuation to show 3 occurs exactly once, then excludes every additional prime factor with a valid order argument.

steps.title: Maximum Cubic Moment
steps.prompt:
Let n ≥ 3 be an integer, and let a₁, a₂, …, aₙ be real numbers satisfying

Σaᵢ = 0  and  Σaᵢ² = 1.

Determine the maximum possible value of Σaᵢ³, and characterize all tuples for which equality holds. Give a rigorous proof.
steps.reference:
The maximum is

(n − 2)/√(n(n − 1)).

Equality holds exactly, up to permutation, for

(a₁, …, aₙ) = (√((n − 1)/n), −1/√(n(n − 1)), …, −1/√(n(n − 1))).

Proof: The feasible set is the intersection of the hyperplane Σaᵢ = 0 with the unit sphere Σaᵢ² = 1, so it is compact and the continuous objective Σaᵢ³ attains a maximum.

At any constrained extremum, the gradients of the two constraints are independent: if (2a₁, …, 2aₙ) were a multiple of (1, …, 1), all aᵢ would be equal, contradicting Σaᵢ = 0 and Σaᵢ² = 1. Hence Lagrange multipliers apply. There exist constants λ and μ such that, for every i,

3aᵢ² = λ + 2μaᵢ.

Thus every aᵢ is a root of the same quadratic equation 3t² − 2μt − λ = 0, so at most two distinct values occur. There cannot be only one distinct value, so there are exactly two.

Suppose the positive value u occurs k times and the negative value v occurs n − k times, where 1 ≤ k ≤ n − 1. The constraints give

ku + (n − k)v = 0,
ku² + (n − k)v² = 1.

Solving with u > 0 > v gives

u = √((n − k)/(kn)),
v = −√(k/(n(n − k))).

Therefore

Σaᵢ³ = ku³ + (n − k)v³
= (n − 2k)/√(nk(n − k)).

For k ≥ n/2 this value is nonpositive, whereas the value for k = 1 is positive. For 1 ≤ k < n/2, write t = k/n. Apart from the positive constant factor 1/√n, the expression is

g(t) = (1 − 2t)/√(t(1 − t)).

On 0 < t < 1/2,

g′(t) = −2/√(t(1 − t)) − (1 − 2t)²/[2(t(1 − t))^(3/2)] < 0.

Hence the expression strictly decreases as k runs from 1 toward n/2, and its maximum occurs at k = 1. Substitution gives

u = √((n − 1)/n),
v = −1/√(n(n − 1)),

and

Σaᵢ³ = (n − 2)/√(n(n − 1)).

The displayed tuple directly satisfies both constraints, so the bound is attained. Strict decrease shows that every maximizing tuple has exactly one entry equal to u and all remaining entries equal to v, up to permutation.
rubric: Derives the sharp maximum (n − 2)/√(n(n − 1)) rather than merely giving a bound.
Rigorously proves that an extremizer has at most two distinct coordinate values and compares all possible multiplicities.
Correctly characterizes every equality case, up to permutation, and verifies that it satisfies the constraints.
